title: What Happens If Humans Had One Eye?
sources: American Academy of Ophthalmology, 'Depth Perception': binocular convergence and stereopsis provide depth; monocular vision uses other cues and can adapt
PMC 11262539 (2024), 'Comparison of Depth-Related Visuomotor Task Performance': dynamic depth-related tasks are harder without binocular viewing
NCBI, 'Induction of Monocular Stereopsis by Altering Focus Distance': the visual system can gain some depth impression through monocular focus changes
American Academy of Ophthalmology, guidance for people with monocular vision: adaptation is possible, but the seeing eye requires protection

lines.text: What happens if humans had only one eye?
At first, your world would look almost normal.
You would still see shapes, colors, and movement.
But you would lose binocular depth perception,
the tiny difference between the images your two eyes receive.
Reaching for a cup, parking a car, or catching a ball could become harder.
You would rely more on shadows, motion, size, and changes in focus.
Those monocular cues give the brain useful clues about distance.
People with one eye often adapt, and many live and move normally.
The biggest change would not be sight, but judging depth at a glance.
